splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that affect criminal liability or punishment.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This matters because it determines whether agencies can effectively expand criminal punishment through interpretive commentary rather than clear textual authority.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Sentencing Guidelines Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary can validly expand the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses not mentioned in the guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions face significantly enhanced sentences under the career-offender provision.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a valid, authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond its plain meaning, so conspiracy convictions cannot serve as career-offender predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one of the criteria is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on the circuit in which they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that meeting any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' effectively as 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b)) when the state statute covers substances not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' is limited to substances controlled under federal law or also encompasses substances controlled only under state law. This affects the career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not federally scheduled.

positions.label: State-controlled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug offense qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines even if the substance is not federally scheduled, because the guideline broadly references 'an offense under state law' without a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Must match federal schedules
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug offense qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. De Jesus Ventura

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's amendments to § 924(c) stacking) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) policy statement validly authorizes such consideration.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes can never contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons,' while others allow courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this by permitting consideration of sentencing changes, but at least the Seventh Circuit has held this exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for sentence reduction, and the Commission's policy statement cannot override this limitation.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly in combination with other factors, and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement validly authorizes this.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or execution of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on the scope of habeas corpus for federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions about conditions or terms of confinement, including First Step Act time-credit disputes. The Supreme Court noted but did not resolve this question in Preiser v. Rodriguez and subsequent cases. The circuits have developed irreconcilable approaches to when habeas is the exclusive remedy versus when civil rights actions are available.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 is available (and may be required) for challenges to BOP decisions affecting the conditions or execution of confinement, including First Step Act time-credit calculations.

positions.label: Civil rights actions permitted alongside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge conditions of confinement through civil rights actions and are not limited to habeas corpus, which is reserved for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release as punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions, or whether revocation sentences must be justified solely by the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release may be based on punishing the defendant for the violating conduct, or must instead be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust inherent in violating release conditions. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows courts expressly to punish defendants for violations, which other circuits view as contrary to the statutory text and Supreme Court guidance.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying their supervised release violations when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Revocation sentences address breach of trust only
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of the court's trust inherent in violating supervised release conditions, not as direct punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the applicable time limit to appeal a Hyde Amendment order (denying attorney's fees in a criminal case) is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged a circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline (30 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline (14 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This affects whether Chapter 7 trustees can sell appreciated assets to satisfy creditors after a good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a) compel the conclusion that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, object, policies, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors in a good-faith conversion.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on the timing requirements for actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing of when assumptions can be selected directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay to multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions must be selected and fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, so long as they are applied to data as of that date, allowing plans to use more current and potentially more accurate assumptions.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sofamor Danek Group v. Brown Group

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, so the supervised release period does not run while the person absconds.

positions.label: No tolling — supervised release runs continuously
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term continues to run regardless of the supervisee's fugitive status.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners cannot raise any previously presented claim regardless of other circumstances; if it does not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) bar applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) bar does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, and that successive § 2255 motions are governed exclusively by § 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standard for evaluating whether candidates can challenge election rules before an election takes place. Adopting a broad rule granting candidates automatic or near-automatic standing would make it far easier to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures nationwide, while denying standing would funnel disputes into post-election litigation.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election rules that affect ballot counting because vote dilution from unlawful ballots constitutes a concrete and particularized injury.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to ballot-counting procedures absent a showing of concrete, particularized injury beyond speculative competitive harm.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as a matter 'too important' to be denied immediate review.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, because delayed review risks irreversible harm to medical privacy. Other circuits have not recognized this category of orders as immediately appealable, creating potential divergence in the scope of the collateral order doctrine.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost absent immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the interest can be adequately vindicated through other means such as protective orders or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, including issues of liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, indicating a potential circuit split on the applicable legal framework for fair treatment in hospitality, retail, and service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that business operators face broader liability for discrimination claims, with more expansive remedies available to aggrieved customers.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards apply to discrimination claims against business operators, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
